query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the alloy composition and thermal processing in steels (specifically by increasing Cr content and suitable post-thermal treatments) enhances the formation of a dense, uniform, Cr-enriched passivation layer (primarily Cr2O3 and associated spinel oxides) that is responsible for improved corrosion resistance in simulated chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels with a baseline low-to-moderate Cr concentration and standard fabrication processes that yield a thinner, non-uniform oxide layer with limited protective properties.
generation.intervention: Manipulate alloying elements by increasing Cr (and potentially minor additions of other elements that stabilize the oxide) and apply controlled post-thermal treatments to promote the in-situ formation of a dense and adherent passive oxide film.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments with controlled pH, temperature, ion concentrations (e.g., Cl−), and where possible, controlled radiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A well-developed, continuous, and defect-free Cr-enriched passivation film (including mixed oxide/spinel phases) on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of Cr during exposure leads to the formation of a protective Cr2O3 (and associated spinel) layer. This layer, due to its density and uniformity, suppresses further oxidation and minimizes pitting corrosion by acting as a physical barrier to aggressive chemical species and radiation-induced damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with enhanced Cr content and optimized thermal processing will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance, increased pitting potentials, and lower corrosion current densities relative to baseline steels. In-situ surface analyses (e.g., XPS, SEM) will confirm a denser and more uniform passivation film.
generation.baseline: Steels with lower Cr content and without the additional thermal treatment, which develop thinner, less uniform oxide layers that offer inferior corrosion resistance under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for steels and related alloys operating under similar corrosive conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. Its validity may be limited if the environmental parameters significantly exceed or deviate from those tested (e.g., extreme radiation flux beyond controlled levels or environments that promote alternative oxide formation pathways).
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the secondary effects of other alloying elements and radiation on the long-term stability and integrity of the passivation film. Additionally, while Cr is predicted to be the dominant contributor, potential synergistic or antagonistic effects from other elements (e.g., Ni, Co) under irradiation require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one with increased Cr content and subjected to controlled post-thermal treatments to encourage passivation layer formation, and a control group with standard composition and processing. Expose both sets to simulated chemical-processing and nuclear environments with defined pH, temperature, Cl− concentration, and controlled radiation dosage. Use in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and surface analyses (XPS, SEM) to monitor passivation film formation.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance (EIS) profiles to assess passive film resistance.
Pitting potential from potentiodynamic polarization curves.
Surface composition and morphology using XPS and SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-enhanced and thermally treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in impedance, pitting potential, or formation of a denser and more uniform passivation film compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis (that optimizing Cr content and thermal processing enhances corrosion resistance via improved passive film formation) will be falsified.

Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

These results indicate that the resistance to pitting of the HEAs is determined exclusively by Cr, and the effect of other elements such as Ni and Co on the passivity is limited. If one compares the pitting potential with those of 304 SS [,], the pitting potential of 304 SS is higher than that in the present results despite having the same PRE, and it increased with the formation of the UFG structure. However, little difference in Epit was observed between the HPT and CG samples, which suggests that UFG formation by HPT has little impact on the protective properties of the passivation film and the corrosion resistance. Figure 10 shows the EDS line profiles for the CG5 and HPT5 specimens after polarization in the passive region (400 mVAg/AgCl) for 2 h in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution. Figure 11 shows the corresponding STEM images and elemental maps. The layer with a high O signal is considered to be the passivation film. A Cr-rich oxide layer was observed on both CG and HPT specimens, which indicates that a stable passivation film can form on both specimens and that Cr is the main passivation former. chosen.lever: manipulation of alloying elements and post-thermal treatments to tune the formation and properties of the surface passivation layer
chosen.technique: a combination of electrochemical corrosion testing (e.g., impedance spectroscopy) with real-time surface characterization (using XPS and SEM)

chosen.why: This study most directly addresses the open mechanistic question by directly isolating the influence of compositional and processing variables on the formation of protective oxide layers.
